Green Loom · Retail catalog

What changed: the product, or permission to sell it?

A product, its store listing, its stock, and its lab certificate change for different reasons. As co-founder, I designed a catalog model and publishing workflow that keeps those responsibilities clear.

Role
Co-founder
Scope
Retail catalog model and operator workflow
Key decision
Separate product identity from store operations and lab evidence
Outcome
Selected design direction, approved wireframe baseline, and a public schema

I — Inspiration

One product carried several different responsibilities

A lab certificate can expire while the product itself stays exactly the same. If both facts live in one undifferentiated record, a catalog can make a change in eligibility look like a change in identity. That distinction became a useful starting point for the catalog model.

A retail catalog looks like a list of products until an operator has to manage it. One product can have multiple packages, different prices and stock at each store, and lab evidence that affects whether it can be offered at all.

Research into the operating workflow, CMS wireframes, product definitions, and external formats exposed conflicting vocabularies. Product form was mixed with regulatory classification. Potency appeared editable on the product even though the laboratory result should be its source. Price and quantity sat beside shared content but changed independently by location.

Georgia’s consumable-hemp rules made these distinctions consequential. Retail sale of hemp flower and leaves is prohibited. Products need a publicly available full-panel certificate of analysis, or COA, contracted within the last 12 months. Labels must provide the results or QR access to them.

Georgia Department of Agriculture retail guidance informed the product-form, evidence, and labeling requirements.

D — Design Process

A certificate can expire without changing the product

I gave the certificate its own Lab Result record and validity period. In the designed publication check, expired evidence blocks the store listing and explains why. The product keeps its identity and content.

Linking replacement evidence should restore eligibility without asking the operator to recreate the product. This separates the rule for offering an item from the record describing what the item is.

D — Design Process

Stock, listings, and lab results change independently

Product holds shared identity and content. Variant identifies a sellable package. Listing controls how a variant is offered at a store. Inventory records quantity and availability. Lab Result holds the certificate.

The interface can bring these facts together while keeping their ownership separate. Changing stock should not require editing the product. Replacing a certificate should not require recreating a store listing.

What could the catalog learn from a lab certificate?

The COA capture workflow begins with the source document. Operators review the extracted results, link them to the applicable product or variant, and use lab-sourced values to seed catalog data. Potency stays traceable to evidence instead of becoming an unrelated editable field.

E — Engagement

Give the model and the workflow a shared vocabulary

Working through the operating workflow and wireframe baseline connected the catalog vocabulary to the decisions an operator needed to make. A shared description, a sellable package, a store offer, stock, and lab evidence could appear together on screen while still having separate responsibilities.

I used those distinctions to connect the product model, publishing checks, and the public schema. The selected design direction and approved baseline supplied a common point of reference. They did not establish that operators had validated the complete workflow; that remained the next step.

A — Action

A first publication and a stock update needed different paths

We compared an object-first approach with a journey-led launchpad and a cross-object work queue. I chose a guided first-publish path with direct catalog and inventory workspaces for returning operators.

First use needs to explain unfamiliar records in a sensible order. Routine work needs fast access to the record that changed. The tradeoff is maintaining both paths without turning every update into another trip through the wizard.

A — Action

Existing data formats didn’t describe the catalog we needed

Research into existing standards and vendor formats did not yield a complete product-data contract for this catalog. We developed and published the versioned Cannabis Product Schema. Its neutral core describes Product, Package, LabResult, Label, and Party. A Georgia hemp profile adds local constraints without embedding them in the core.

The schema validates exchanged data. The Retail application still needs its own operator-facing records for editing, publishing, and adjusting stock. Keeping those jobs separate avoids making a data format dictate the entire workflow.

S — Success

We had a selected direction and a published schema

The work produced a selected information architecture, an approved wireframe baseline, and a published schema. COA import and the complete publication gate remain designed workflows; later high-fidelity work is a candidate for operator validation.

The next test is whether operators can create and maintain the right records without losing the connection to their evidence. My takeaway: a regulated workflow gets clearer when each record has a distinct job and the interface explains what blocks the next action.

I’m happy to walk through the catalog model or the publishing decisions.
